newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan scandal could jolt financial firms to reform.
newsitem.headline: Japan scandal could jolt financial firms to reform.

text.p: Japan's racketeer payoff scandal is hitting some top firms' credibility hard, but ultimately could give Tokyo's banks and brokerages just the jolt they need to reform their wayward and uncompetitive ways.
That said, however, the changes are likely to take quite some time and weaker institutions could well find the lesson in corporate ethics and competition painful, if not debilitating.

The Finance Ministry on Wednesday announced its stiffest-ever penalties against giant Nomura Securities Co Ltd and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd, both involved in the scandal over payoffs to a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer.

The affair, which on the same day ensnared Yamaichi Securities Co, the weakest of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages, is unfolding just as Tokyo initiates drastic reforms to boost competition to its long-protected financial industry.

Prosecutors and securities watchdog inspectors raided Yamaichi offices seeking evidence of suspected illegal deals with Ryuichi Koike, the sokaiya at the heart of the Nomura-DKB affair. A government source told reporters Yamaichi had generally admitted to the misdeeds.

Big Four brokerage Daiwa Securities, however, denied media reports that it too had illegally compensated Koike for losses while Nikko Securities said it did not think it had conducted any illegal transactions. Both securities houses are currently under investigation by a government watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC).
Still, concern persists that the scandal saga could drag on for months as authorities probe other institutions, driving Big Four clients into the arms of foreign rivals.
The penalties against Nomura and DKB included the suspension of some key businesses until the end of the year and for DKB a ban on fresh overseas business other than lending for a full year.
The steps will hit Nomura's profits harder than DKB's and could give rival foreign brokers a chance to grab more business.
"I think the scandal has worked to some extent to the advantage of foreigners. But now they have to press home that advantage," said Brian Waterhouse, analyst at HSBC James Capel.
Some Japanese analysts were even gloomier.

"Corporate clients will not return to Nomura and the scandal will probably spread to Yamaichi, Daiwa and Nikko. The clients who defect from the Big Four are likely to go to foreign brokerages and it will be the foreign firms who are laughing," said an analyst at a Japanese brokerage.

Still, some analysts said the sweeping management shake-ups at Nomura and DKB prompted by the scandal give the two firms a golden opportunity to reform and adopt strategies needed for success as deregulation proceeds. Others firms will likely follow suit.

"It (the scandal) hurts their profits over the next year, but in terms of the 'Big Bang' (financial reforms), this forces them to restructure more aggressively," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at J.P. Morgan in Tokyo.
"What the first oil shock did to Japanese manufacturers, this is now engineering for the financial sector," Koll said.
"The result is going to be...that they become globally competitive. But it took 15 years for the manufacturers and it may take as long for the financial companies as well."
In tandem with the planned Big Bang reforms, the scandal could also also force authorities, for years now under fire for alleged lax supervision of financial institutions, to tighten surveillance.

The Finance Ministry promised on Wednesday to beef up its supervision and a new financial supervision agency is to be set up next year. Politicians, meanwhile, have already pledged bigger fines and longer jail terms for corporate lawbreakers.

"This will galvanise authorities to review the current laws and penalties for financial impropriety and bring them up to levels in the United States and other advanced countries," Waterhouse said, adding he still had "grave doubts about officials' ability to control and monitor adequately".

Shorter-term, however, if Yamaichi ultimately suffers penalties for its alleged involvement in the scandal, the brokerage would find it far more difficult to absorb harsh punishment than the mammoth Nomura, analysts said.
"They are a quite a weak institution and it might be a very costly example," said James McGinnis, a financial analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson International.
"I think the result (of the scandal) ultimately is a positive one if they move to more transparency, but it could be a rough ride getting there," McGinnis added.
